title: Yom Kippur: the fast
hookLine: twenty-five hours without food, drink or leather shoes, like angels for a day

lines: A DAY FULL OF SMALL REACHING.
cards: A coffee. A snack. A glass of water.
A phone. A mirror. An ordinary day is full of small reaching, most of it automatic.
Yom Kippur puts all of that down. No food, not even water. No leather shoes.
No lotion, no washing up. From just before sunset to after nightfall the next day: about twenty-five hours. Some wear white and spend most of the day in the synagogue, standing, praying, remembering.

teach.h: YOM KIPPUR: THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.
teach.b: Yom Kippur means the Day of Atonement. The word kippur comes from a root often understood as covering, or wiping clean.

The Torah says: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." And it gives one instruction for the body: "ye shall afflict your souls."
The rabbis read that as five things to go without: eating and drinking, washing, anointing with oils, wearing leather shoes, and marital intimacy. Why leather?
One explanation: leather shoes were the fine, comfortable ones, so on this day people walk a little closer to the ground. And why white?
An old idea says that on Yom Kippur Jews are like angels: angels don't eat or drink, they stand, and they wear white. So for one day, people set aside the body's needs and stand like them.
Two things matter as much as the fast. First, the fast is never allowed to endanger a life.

Anyone who is ill, pregnant with complications, or at risk is told to eat, and Jewish law calls eating then a duty, not a failure. Young children don't fast. Second, Yom Kippur has a limit that surprises people.
The Mishnah teaches that this day atones for wrongs between a person and God.

teach.h: FIRST, GO TO THE PERSON YOU HURT.
teach.b: For wrongs between one person and another, it doesn't, until you've gone to the person you hurt and tried to make it right.

teach.h: FROM ALL YOUR SINS SHALL YE BE CLEAN.
teach.b: So in the days before, the custom is to call, text or knock on doors and ask: if I hurt you this year, forgive me. The hungry day in the synagogue comes after the harder conversation.

how: On Yom Kippur, many Jews fast for about twenty-five hours, avoid leather shoes and washing, wear white, and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer. Those whose health is at risk are required to eat, and young children do not fast.

o: the Day of Atonement: a day of fasting and prayer
a holy day kept only by rabbis and priests
a day of feasting to close out the old year

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: read as five things set aside

s: everyone must fast on Yom Kippur, even if they're ill
anyone whose health is at risk is required to eat. saving a life comes first.
Yom Kippur alone atones for hurting another person
the Mishnah says you must first go to the person and make it right.
leather shoes are traditionally not worn on Yom Kippur
it's one of the five things set aside for the day.

games.q: it's the week before Yom Kippur. you know you hurt a friend this year. what does Jewish teaching say comes first?
o: fast extra hard and pray about it.
go to your friend and ask forgiveness.
wait and see if they bring it up.
games.why: the Mishnah teaches that Yom Kippur doesn't atone for wrongs between people until you've made peace with the person you hurt.

practice: Set down one small comfort for these few minutes, the second coffee, the scroll, the snack you don't need, never your meals or medicine, and notice what it feels like not to reach.
Then think of one person you may have hurt this year and just hold their name; you don't have to call yet.

wordCard.voice: Yom Kippur. The Day of Atonement: twenty-five hours of fasting and prayer, after first making peace with the people you've hurt.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Day of Atonement; the Torah calls it yom ha-kippurim.
